spark.summary: Distributing incoming network connections or application requests across healthy backend servers to maximize throughput, minimize tail latency, and survive node failures seamlessly.
spark.keyTakeaway: Match the balancing layer and algorithm to your traffic: use L4 (Maglev/DSR) for raw packet scale, L7 (Envoy/ALB) for gRPC/HTTP routing, and Power-of-Two-Choices (P2C) + EWMA to crush p99 tail latency.

concept.whyItMatters: A single server has hard CPU, NIC, and failure boundaries; without load balancing, one overloaded instance or crashed AZ takes down the whole service. Worse, naive round-robin load balancing sends heavy requests to already-busy nodes, spiking p99 tail latency even when cluster average CPU sits at 40%.
whenToUse: Horizontally scaling stateless APIs, microservices, or LLM inference replicas across multiple pods, VMs, or Availability Zones.
Zero-downtime deployments (blue/green, canary traffic splitting) and automatic outlier ejection when a backend node degrades.
Multiplexed protocols like HTTP/2 and gRPC, where L4 TCP-level balancing pins an entire long-lived connection to one backend pod.
whenNotToUse: Single-node local development or tiny internal tools where a single reverse proxy (Caddy/NGINX) without multi-AZ health meshes suffices.
Stateful leader-only databases (e.g., primary PostgreSQL writes) where arbitrary request spraying breaks consistency—route via service discovery or read-replica pools instead.
Blindly stacking multiple redundant L7 proxies in series when each hop adds TLS termination, serialization, and debugging overhead.
keyPoints: **L4 (Transport)** balancers route on `(src_ip, src_port, dst_ip, dst_port, proto)` using IPVS/eBPF/Maglev at millions of PPS; **L7 (Application)** balancers terminate TLS/HTTP to route on headers, paths, and gRPC frames.

**gRPC / HTTP/2 Trap**: Because HTTP/2 multiplexes thousands of RPCs over one TCP connection, an L4 balancer sends all traffic to a single backend; you must use L7 load balancing or client-side balancing.

**Power of Two Choices (P2C) + Peak EWMA** (used by Envoy and Linkerd) samples 2 random backends and picks the one with lower active requests or exponentially weighted moving average latency—cutting tail latency dramatically over Round Robin.
Combine **active health checks** (`/healthz` every 5s) with **passive outlier detection** (ejecting a pod for 30s after 3 consecutive 5xx/timeouts) to catch gray failures.

**Consistent Hashing** (Ketama / Maglev) maps keys (`user_id`, `session_id`, `cache_key`) to the same backend with minimal remapping (`1/N` keys) on node churn—vital for stateful caches and LLM KV-cache affinity.

examples.title: Fixing gRPC Hot-Spotting Behind an AWS NLB
examples.scenario: A microservices team scaled a Go gRPC service from 4 to 20 pods behind a Layer-4 Network Load Balancer, yet 2 pods hit 100% CPU while 18 pods sat idle.
examples.outcome: Long-lived HTTP/2 connections from upstream clients stayed pinned at the TCP layer; migrating to an Envoy L7 ingress (with P2C least-request) rebalanced per-RPC and dropped p99 latency from 420 ms to 38 ms.

examples.title: KV-Cache-Aware Routing for vLLM Inference
examples.scenario: An LLM platform routed multi-turn chat requests round-robin across 8 vLLM GPU replicas, forcing every turn to recompute the 6,000-token system prompt KV cache.
examples.outcome: Switching to L7 consistent hashing on `conversation_id` (with bounded load max 1.25x average) raised GPU prefix-cache hit rates to 88% and doubled cluster tokens-per-second.

tradeOffs.pro: L4 handles massive packet rates (>10M PPS) with near-zero CPU overhead and preserves client IPs via Direct Server Return (DSR).
tradeOffs.con: Cannot inspect HTTP paths, JWTs, or gRPC requests, and cannot rebalance multiplexed HTTP/2 connections.

tradeOffs.pro: Round Robin is stateless, O(1), and zero-coordination across distributed balancer replicas.
tradeOffs.con: Ignores heterogeneous request costs (e.g., a 5s PDF export vs a 5ms health check), causing severe head-of-line queuing on slow nodes.

tradeOffs.pro: Maximizes local in-memory cache and KV-cache hit rates by pinning keys to specific backends.
tradeOffs.con: A viral 'hot key' can overload its assigned shard unless mitigated with bounded loads or key salting.

failureModes.name: Herd / Cascading Failure via Health Check Storm
failureModes.description: A backend slows down under load, fails `/healthz` timeouts, gets ejected, and dumps its traffic onto the remaining 4 nodes—causing them to fail `/healthz` too in a domino collapse.
failureModes.mitigation: Cap max ejection percentage (e.g., Envoy `max_ejection_percent: 50%`) and panic-threshold routing (fall back to all hosts if healthy % drops below 50%).

failureModes.name: Slow-Start Cold Cache Spike
failureModes.description: A newly booted pod passes `/healthz` immediately and receives full traffic before JIT compilation or local caches warm up, timing out user requests.
failureModes.mitigation: Enable slow-start mode (linearly ramping weight over 30–60s) and separate `/livez` from `/readyz`.

failureModes.name: Cross-AZ Bandwidth & Latency Tax
failureModes.description: A cluster-wide balancer sprays requests across 3 Availability Zones evenly, adding 1–2 ms per hop and $0.01–$0.02/GB inter-AZ data transfer fees.
failureModes.mitigation: Enable zone-aware / topology-aware routing so traffic prefers same-AZ backends unless local capacity is exhausted.

failureModes.name: Sticky Session / Consistent Hash Imbalance
failureModes.description: One enterprise tenant generates 40% of traffic on a single `tenant_id` hash bucket, saturating one pod.
failureModes.mitigation: Use Consistent Hashing with Bounded Loads (cap node load at 1.25x mean) or salt hot keys across `k` virtual buckets.

commonMistakes: Putting gRPC or HTTP/2 clients behind an L4 TCP load balancer without client-side balancing or an L7 proxy.
Implementing `/healthz` that queries the primary database—turning a transient DB hiccup into total fleet-wide pod eviction.
Disabling connection keep-alives between L7 proxy and backends, forcing a fresh TCP + TLS handshake on every internal hop.
Forgetting graceful draining (`SIGTERM` -> fail `/readyz` -> wait `preStop` 15–30s) during rolling deploys, causing 502 Bad Gateway spikes.
Relying on DNS round-robin alone for failover—clients and JVMs cache DNS TTLs aggressively and ignore dead IPs.

sections.content:
## The idea

At its core, load balancing solves a **distributed scheduling problem**: given `M` concurrent clients and `N` heterogeneous, failure-prone backends, map each connection or request to a healthy backend so no single node saturates while total throughput and tail latency stay optimal.

Production architectures almost always use a **two-tier pipeline**:
1. **Edge L4 Tier (Anycast BGP + ECMP -> Maglev/IPVS)**: Statelessly hashes 5-tuples across L7 proxy nodes at line rate without terminating TLS.
2. **L7 Proxy Tier (Envoy / NGINX / ALB)**: Terminates TLS, inspects HTTP/gRPC metadata, applies rate limits and circuit breakers, and dispatches individual requests using **Power of Two Choices (P2C)** or **Consistent Hashing**.

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace a single gRPC API request hitting a high-traffic Kubernetes cluster:

1. **DNS & Anycast BGP**: Client resolves `api.example.com` to an Anycast VIP announced by 3 regional PoPs; ECMP routes the TCP SYN packet to an L4 Maglev/IPVS node.
2. **L4 -> L7 Dispatch**: Maglev hashes the 5-tuple consistently to `envoy-ingress-04` (so even if another L4 node reboots, the TCP flow stays pinned to `envoy-ingress-04`).
3. **L7 Termination & Auth**: `envoy-ingress-04` terminates TLS 1.3, parses the HTTP/2 `:path` (`/inference.v1/Generate`), and checks token-bucket rate limits.
4. **P2C-EWMA Backend Selection**: Envoy picks 2 healthy pods from the 24-pod `inference` endpoint list (`pod-07` with Peak EWMA 18 ms vs `pod-19` with Peak EWMA 94 ms) and forwards the RPC over a pre-warmed HTTP/2 connection pool to `pod-07`.
5. **Outlier Protection**: If `pod-07` returns 3 consecutive `503`/`DEADLINE_EXCEEDED` responses within 10s, Envoy's passive outlier detector ejects `pod-07` for 30s without waiting for the next active `/readyz` poll.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / Algorithms: P2C, Peak EWMA, and Consistent Hashing
sections.content:
## Algorithms: P2C, Peak EWMA, and Consistent Hashing

- **Power of Two Choices (P2C)**: Checking all `N` backends per request takes `O(N)` and causes 'herd' behavior when distributed proxies all see the same single least-loaded node and stampede it simultaneously. P2C picks 2 backends uniformly at random (`O(1)`) and routes to the better one—mathematically reducing maximum queue depth from `O(log N / log log N)` to `O(log log N)`.
- **Peak EWMA**: Active-connection count alone misses a degraded pod that fails fast or stalls on GC pauses. Peak EWMA tracks each backend's exponentially weighted moving average latency multiplied by `(active_requests + 1)`, automatically steering traffic away from slow or throttling nodes.
- **Maglev & Ring Hash**: When routing stateful caches or LLM prefix caches, Ring Hash (Ketama) or Google Maglev builds a lookup table where adding/removing 1 of `N` nodes remaps only `~1/N` of keys instead of invalidating the entire cache.

## Load balancing algorithms compared

| Algorithm | Complexity | Tail Latency (p99) | Cache Affinity | Best Use Case |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Round Robin** | O(1) | Poor under variable load | None | Homogeneous, fixed-cost static file servers |
| **Least Connections** | O(N) or heap | Good (single proxy) | None | Long-lived WebSockets or variable-duration DB queries |
| **P2C + Peak EWMA** | O(1) | Excellent (-30–50% p99) | None | Multi-proxy L7 microservices (Envoy, Linkerd) |
| **Consistent Hash (Maglev/Ring)** | O(1) – O(log N) | Good (with bounded load) | High (~1/N churn) | Redis/CDN shards, stateful actors, LLM KV-cache routing |
| **IP Hash (5-Tuple)** | O(1) | Poor for HTTP/2 | Connection-level | L4 edge distribution across stateless L7 proxies |

## Failure modes

1. **Retry Storms Amplifying Outages**: If 3 microservice hops each retry 3 times on timeout, a single slow downstream DB receives `3 * 3 * 3 = 27x` normal traffic. *Fix*: Enforce retry budgets (max 10–20% of active requests) and per-request deadline propagation (`grpc-timeout`).
2. **Connection Pool Exhaustion / Ephemeral Port Starvation**: Opening a new TCP connection per upstream request exhausts the 65,535 ephemeral ports (`TIME_WAIT`) at high RPS. *Fix*: Enable HTTP/1.1 keep-alive / HTTP/2 multiplexing and tune `tcp_tw_reuse`.
3. **Thundering Herd on Pod Restart**: All new pods register simultaneously and get hit before warming up. *Fix*: Use slow-start weight ramping and jittered health-check intervals.
4. **L4 Asymmetric Routing Drops**: Under Direct Server Return (DSR), misconfigured VIP loopback interfaces or strict `rp_filter` kernel settings silently drop return packets. *Fix*: Set `net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter=2` (loose mode) and automate VIP loopback provisioning.

## Zero-downtime draining and zone awareness

Most 502/504 errors during deployments happen because the orchestrator kills a pod before the load balancer stops sending it traffic:

- **Decoupled Readiness**: On `SIGTERM`, the app immediately flips `/readyz` to `503` (while keeping `/livez` `200`), sends `Connection: close` or HTTP/2 `GOAWAY` frames, and waits `15–30s` (`terminationGracePeriodSeconds > preStop + drain`) so in-flight requests finish cleanly.
- **Zone-Aware Routing**: Configure Envoy/K8s Topology Aware Hints so proxies route within the same Availability Zone whenever local capacity >=80% of demand, eliminating cross-AZ latency and data-transfer bills.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Use L7 load balancing (Envoy/ALB/NGINX) for HTTP/2 and gRPC; reserve L4 (NLB/IPVS/Maglev) for edge TCP/UDP scale.
- [ ] Configure P2C + Least-Request or Peak EWMA for heterogeneous API workloads, and Consistent Hashing with bounded loads for cache/LLM-prefix affinity.
- [ ] Pair shallow `/readyz` probes (no external DB calls) with passive outlier detection (`max_ejection_percent <= 50%`).
- [ ] Enforce `GOAWAY` + `preStop` sleep (15–30s) on `SIGTERM` so rolling deploys drop zero in-flight requests.
- [ ] Enable retry budgets (10–20% cap) and end-to-end deadline propagation to prevent retry storms.
- [ ] Turn on zone-aware routing to avoid unnecessary cross-AZ latency and egress charges.

questions.title: Consistent Hashing Node Membership Changes
questions.prompt: What is the primary advantage of Consistent Hashing over standard modulo hashing (hash(K) mod N) when scaling cache cluster nodes?

options.text: It encrypts cache keys using AES-256 before hashing.
options.explanation: Consistent hashing is an allocation algorithm, not encryption.

options.text: Adding or removing a node only remaps K/N keys rather than invalidating almost all cached keys across the entire cluster.
options.explanation: Correct! Only 1/N keys are remapped on cluster membership changes.

rubric.excellent: Identifies minimal key remapping (K/N keys) and prevention of cache stampede on node scale events.
rubric.gap: Confuses hashing with encryption.

questions.sampleSolution: Consistent hashing minimizes key remapping during node additions/removals, re-allocating only K/N keys.
questions.explanation: Standard modulo hashing remaps ~100% of keys when N changes, causing massive cache invalidation.

interviewProblems.title: Stateful Voice Socket Load Balancer
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: You are designing the gateway load balancer for a real-time voice chat application serving 10,000,000 concurrent WebSocket connections. When a backend voice server crashes or scales up, how do you minimize connection drops and avoid server overload?

dimensions.name: Layer 4 vs Layer 7 Selection
dimensions.description: Using L4 Maglev/IPVS for socket throughput and L7 Envoy for HTTP routing.

dimensions.name: Consistent Ring Virtual Nodes
dimensions.description: Using virtual nodes (vnodes) to prevent traffic hotspots.

interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Use Layer 4 Maglev consistent hashing for incoming TCP WebSocket handshakes. Use virtual nodes (vnodes=256) per voice server to evenly distribute connections and ensure scaling up or down only migrates 1/N connections.
commonPitfalls: Using simple round-robin which breaks sticky WebSocket sessions.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Distributing incoming network connections or application requests across healthy backend servers to maximize throughput, minimize tail latency, and survive node failures seamlessly.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Health & Outlier Plane applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Backend Pool.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Backend Pool experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Cap max ejection percentage (e.g., Envoy `max_ejection_percent: 50%`) and panic-threshold routing (fall back to all hosts if healthy % drops below 50%).

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Match the balancing layer and algorithm to your traffic: use L4 (Maglev/DSR) for raw packet scale, L7 (Envoy/ALB) for gRPC/HTTP routing, and Power-of-Two-Choices (P2C) + EWMA to crush p99 tail latency.
Avoid trap: Putting gRPC or HTTP/2 clients behind an L4 TCP load balancer without client-side balancing or an L7 proxy.
Avoid trap: Implementing `/healthz` that queries the primary database—turning a transient DB hiccup into total fleet-wide pod eviction.
When to reach for it: Horizontally scaling stateless APIs, microservices, or LLM inference replicas across multiple pods, VMs, or Availability Zones.
When to reach for it: Zero-downtime deployments (blue/green, canary traffic splitting) and automatic outlier ejection when a backend node degrades.

putItTogether.title: Putting Load Balancing Together
putItTogether.summary: Match the balancing layer and algorithm to your traffic: use L4 (Maglev/DSR) for raw packet scale, L7 (Envoy/ALB) for gRPC/HTTP routing, and Power-of-Two-Choices (P2C) + EWMA to crush p99 tail latency.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Load Balancing before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Long-lived HTTP/2 connections from upstream clients stayed pinned at the TCP layer; migrating to an Envoy L7 ingress (with P2C least-request) rebalanced per-RPC and dropped p99 latency from 420 ms to 38 ms.
